transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-06-17
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Liao (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Das (Redwood Solutions Eng), Maya Patel (Bluefjord Product), Lucas Hwang (Bluefjord Platform), Aaron Chen (Bluefjord Data Eng), Tara O'Neill (Bluefjord FinOps)

Summary (auto): Quick product demo of Redwood Console focusing on route-level usage analytics and cost attribution. Team covered how per-route dashboards map to billing, how to configure routing policies (hosted vs dedicated), and data/security requirements for a pilot. Agreed next steps for data export and pricing.

Topics: Console overview; per-route cost breakdown; telemetry exports; dedicated capacity vs hosted fallbacks; SSO/KMS/audit logs; pilot scoping

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan Liao: Hey everyone, uh thanks for joining. I think we have about 45-ish minutes, we'll run through the console and then leave time for questions. Priya's gonna take the demo, and I'll jump in on pricing and the pilot stuff.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Cool, thanks Jordan. Hi Maya, Lucas, Aaron, Tara. I'll share my screen — okay can everyone see the Redwood Console? I see a thumbs up in chat, great.

[00:31] Maya Patel: Yep, we can see it. Looks cleaner than the deck.

[00:36] Priya Nair: Great. So top left is the usage overview — overall tokens, embedding units, and request volume. The thing we focus on here is the Routes tab, this is where you map logical application endpoints to billing lanes and model variants. For example you can route low-latency chat traffic to a fast (and higher cost) lane, and background summarization to a cheaper quantized variant.

[01:05] Lucas Hwang: Quick clarifying q — when you say "route", is that per-endpoint in our app or per-customer? We do both.

[01:12] Priya Nair: Good question — you can do both. Routes are arbitrary keys you pass with the request — a route name can represent an endpoint, a product tier, or a customer id. The console shows per-route telemetry so you can slice by route and see cost, latency P95, and error rates.

[01:30] Aaron Chen: How fine-grained is the cost attribution? We need to show chargebacks to internal teams down to the route level, ideally daily.

[01:37] Priya Nair: We export per-token cost and per-request overhead, aggregated by route and time-window. The console has a per-route cost breakdown page and you can export CSVs or connect the billing API to your FinOps tools.

[01:50] Tara O'Neill: Do you do anything to adjust cost for batching or KV cache effects? We saw big cost swings when we turned on batching in our tests.

[01:58] Priya Nair: Yes — great call. The Console shows both raw token usage and effective unit cost after cache and batching. There's a section called "Optimize recommendations" that will flag when batching is lowering unit cost but raising tail latency. It suggests knob changes — batch size, max latency, or model quantization profile.

[02:22] Jordan Liao: Also to add— those recommendations are based on observed per-route profiles. If a route is highly prefix-shared, KV cache gives big wins and the Console will show implied savings. Sometimes the transcriber calls that K-V cash, right? — uh KC cash — the transcription ok.

[02:36] Maya Patel: (laughs) we've got transcription artifacts in our notes too.

[02:41] Priya Nair: Jumping to a sample route, here's "customer_chat_prod" — you can see tokens/day, avg latency, and a model mix (gpt-open-13b-qa / gpt-open-13b-quant). The cost bar stacks show model unit cost, infra overhead, and cache-adjusted savings.

[03:05] Lucas Hwang: That stack is useful. Does the infra overhead include networking and OS GPU reservation?

[03:11] Priya Nair: We include reserved capacity amortization for Dedicated lanes and a small platform fee for hosted. Networking egress isn't included unless it's tied to token delivery — but we can show separate egress buckets if you push that telemetry.

[03:26] Aaron Chen: For our finances we need daily CSVs with route, model, tokens, effective cost, and tag mappings. Is that available?

[03:33] Priya Nair: Absolutely — CSV export, scheduled reports, and a connector to common warehouses (S3, BigQuery) are available. I'll capture that as an action item.

[03:44] Samir Das: If I can interject — one thing customers like is the route change audit trail; we'll show who changed a route's routing policy and when. It's captured in the audit logs, which you can pipe to your SIEM.

[03:58] Maya Patel: Audit logs — yes, that matters for us. Can you confirm retention and SSO?

[04:04] Jordan Liao: Sure — we support SAML/SSO via your IdP, RBAC roles for teams, and audit log retention is configurable (30/90/365 days). For Private deployments you can have customer-managed log retention and syslog streaming.

[04:20] Lucas Hwang: On Private — we have constraints around networking and HSM for keys. Do you support KMS/HSM integrations?

[04:27] Priya Nair: Yes, for Private or Dedicated we integrate with KMS providers and HSM-backed key stores. You'll be able to manage a key per workspace and we provide guidance for envelope encryption.

[04:39] Aaron Chen: Any SOC/compliance artifacts we can get? ISO, SOC2?

[04:44] Jordan Liao: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 docs — I'll share the security packet after the meeting. For Private deployments we also support customer audits and can provide deployment diagrams/controls.

[04:58] Priya Nair: Back to Console — here's the route heatmap. It shows traffic peaks by hour, and if you click on a spike it drills into requests and model version. This is helpful for SLO retros and for deciding capacity commitments.

[05:16] Maya Patel: Could you show an example where a route was auto-routed to a fallback model during a capacity event? We want to understand graceful degradation.

[05:22] Priya Nair: Yeah — here's a demo of a canary and a fallback policy. We set a rule: primary model node group targets p50 < 120ms, fallback to a cheaper model if p95 > 600ms or if queue depth exceeds threshold. The Console will annotate the timeline with the policy change.

[05:40] Lucas Hwang: How does the fallback affect semantics — do you get different outputs from the cheaper model, and do you get alerts when fallback happens?

[05:46] Priya Nair: You will. There's a quality regression monitor you can tie to prompt sets; when a fallback happens it flags regressions against baseline prompts and sends alerts to Slack or an incident channel.

[06:00] Aaron Chen: For billing, if a fallback model is cheaper, is the cost applied retroactively to the request? Or is it recorded per-request at the time of execution?

[06:08] Jordan Liao: It's recorded at execution time — so the billing reflects which model actually served the request. The per-route view will show model mix and attributable cost.

[06:18] Maya Patel: Can we gate certain routes to dedicated capacity? For our premium customers we need isolation guarantees.

[06:23] Priya Nair: Yes — Routes can be bound to a Dedicated pool. You can pin model versions and routing policies to that pool. If the Dedicated pool is out of capacity you can configure fallback to hosted but with a notice and rate limiting.

[06:38] Tara O'Neill: Pricing question — how do you price dedicated pools vs hosted per-token? Our finance team wants predictable monthly commits.

[06:45] Jordan Liao: Dedicated is subscription/reserved capacity — you commit to a set of GPUs or throughput and we price a monthly reservation plus a small overage per token. Hosted is pay-as-you-go per token with tiered volume discounts. We'll send a tailored scenario comparing your peak qps and projected tokens for both.

[06:59] Lucas Hwang: Mentioned competitors earlier — if we use Bedrock or OpenAI now, how do migrations or dual-write look like?

[07:08] Priya Nair: The Console supports multi-backend routing. You can set routing rules to send some traffic to external providers and some to Redwood so you can do shadowing and A/B comparisons. We also provide adapters for common request shapes.

[07:24] Maya Patel: Ok good. On the technical side, we want to run a small pilot — maybe 1% of traffic for 2 weeks — can you recommend an instrumentation plan?

[07:33] Priya Nair: Yes. Typical pilot plan: 1) Send us an anonymized traffic sample (headers + route keys + timing) 2) Set up a route in your app to send 1% of production to Redwood with identical payloads for comparison, 3) Enable prefix & KV caching on the pilot lanes, 4) We'll run a short benchmark and provide unit-cost delta and latency percentiles.

[07:56] Aaron Chen: For the traffic sample what fields do you need? We have PII constraints.

[08:02] Samir Das: We only need request metadata — route, token counts, timestamps, and a sample prompt set. We can sign an NDA and provide a data handling checklist.

[08:12] Tara O'Neill: Is there any chance the console shows incorrect attribution if caching skews the token counts? We had trouble reconciling local cache and server-side cache with other providers.

[08:21] Priya Nair: Great point — the Console shows both raw tokens and cache-normalized tokens. We surface a reconciliation view with event-level logs if you need to reconcile billing.

[08:34] Maya Patel: Can we see a historical example where per-route cost suddenly spiked and how you debugged it?

[08:40] Priya Nair: Sure, here's a case study: a customer turned on a higher temperature model for a route, which increased token usage via longer generations. The Console showed a step in avg tokens per request and a correlated increase in cost. We rolled back the model, and the regulator alerts triggered. The timeline and drill-down made it obvious.

[09:06] Lucas Hwang: Any limits on retention for per-request logs for debugging? We may need longer retention for legal/compliance.

[09:12] Jordan Liao: For Hosted we have standard retention tiers; for Dedicated/Private you can configure longer retention and export to your storage. We'll include the retention table in the security packet.

[09:25] Aaron Chen: For the CSV exports — can we include our internal tags (team, feature, customer id) so the console maps them to routes?

[09:33] Priya Nair: Yes — you can pass metadata tags with each request and we surface them in the per-route view and CSV. We also have a tag-mapping UI to normalize tag names.

[09:45] Maya Patel: Walk me through how the per-route dashboard is constructed — is it a composition of widgets we can save and share?

[09:51] Priya Nair: Exactly — widgets for cost, latency, model mix, and quality signals. You can save dashboards, set a default for your org, and share with read-only links.

[10:03] Samir Das: I'll show an example alert configuration — you can tie a quality regression to a specific prompt set and have it create an incident in PagerDuty.

[10:12] Maya Patel: Nice. One last question from my side — does Redwood provide per-route recommendations to reduce cost while keeping quality? Like suggesting a quant model with a simulated quality delta?

[10:21] Priya Nair: Yes — Optimize recommendations will simulate how a quantized model changes output variance for your prompt set and provide an estimated cost delta. We provide an expected regression % and you can run a small human eval.

[10:36] Lucas Hwang: How long does it take to onboard a pilot from our side? We can allocate an engineer but want a timeline.

[10:42] Jordan Liao: From handshake to pilot we typically do 1-2 weeks: initial data exchange (2-3 days), configuration and routing (2-4 days), then a 1-2 week pilot window. For Dedicated it's longer because of capacity provisioning.

[10:58] Maya Patel: Ok sounds reasonable. Any blockers we should be aware of?

[11:02] Priya Nair: If you need Private deployment or HSM integration that's an extra ops step. Also if your prompts contain high-risk data we'll recommend a Private mode or dedicated lanes with strict key controls.

[11:14] Aaron Chen: One more technical — do you support streaming responses and function/tool calls? We use streaming for chat latency.

[11:20] Priya Nair: Yes streaming is supported in the hosted API and in Dedicated; function/tool-calling is supported in the request contract. The console will show streaming metrics separately (time to first token, tokens per second).

[11:33] Jordan Liao: Alright let's do a quick recap of next steps — Jordan to send security packet and tailored pricing; Priya to share exports and dashboard JSON; Maya/Aaron to share traffic sample and SLOs; schedule pilot kickoff for week of 6/28.

[11:50] Maya Patel: We'll get that traffic sample over, anonymized — thanks everyone.

[11:55] Lucas Hwang: Appreciate the demo. A couple of internal folks want a deeper dive into retention and audit logs, can we schedule a follow-up security call?

[12:03] Jordan Liao: Totally — I'll set that up with our security lead.

[12:07] Tara O'Neill: Thanks all.

[12:10] Priya Nair: Thanks, bye everyone.
